entities.name: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, originating in Japan around the late 10th century, is one of the oldest known monogatari (narratives) and remains a cornerstone of Japanese folklore. This narrative, often regarded as the first example of science fiction in literature, tells the story of a bamboo cutter who finds a tiny, radiant girl inside a bamboo stalk. The tale intricately weaves themes of love, loss, and the ephemeral nature of life, capturing the essence of Heian-era aesthetics and values. Its significance lies not only in its narrative but also in its reflection of the cultural and philosophical currents of its time, influencing both literature and visual arts in Japan and beyond.

The story unfolds with the bamboo cutter discovering the celestial Kaguya-hime, who is raised in his household. As she grows, suitors from across the land are drawn to her beauty but face insurmountable challenges set by Kaguya-hime herself, who ultimately reveals her identity as a lunar being. The narrative culminates with her departure to the Moon, leaving behind a profound sense of longing and unfulfilled love. This tale encapsulates the rich interplay of myth and human experience, intertwining elements of Shinto beliefs with Buddhist philosophies prevalent during the Heian period.

The legacy of The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter extends far beyond its initial creation; it laid foundational motifs for future Japanese literature and inspired countless adaptations in various forms, including film, theater, and anime. Its themes resonate with the universal human experience, making it relevant across cultures and eras. Notably, the story's influence can be seen in modern works, such as Studio Ghibli's animated film "The Tale of the Princess Kaguya," which reinterprets the original narrative, thereby introducing it to new generations.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (Japanese: 竹取物語, Taketori Monogatari) is the earliest surviving Japanese prose narrative, composed c. 909–910 CE (with some scholars proposing 850–950 CE), written in Chinese characters (kanji) rather than in the kana that would later characterise Heian women's literature, and attributed to an unknown author. It is the founding text of Japanese narrative prose — referred to by Murasaki Shikibu in the Tale of Genji as 'the ancestor of all tales' (monogatari no oya) — and one of the earliest examples of science fiction in world literature.

The tale narrates the discovery by an old bamboo cutter (Taketori no Okina) of a tiny luminous girl inside a shining bamboo stalk, whom he raises as his daughter, naming her Kaguya-hime ('Shining Princess'). As she grows, her extraordinary beauty attracts five noble suitors (including the Emperor himself), each of whom she sends on impossible quests for legendary treasures — a robe of fire-rat fur, the jewelled branch of the island of Hōrai, the stone begging bowl of the Buddha, the jewel from a dragon's neck, and the cowrie-shell born from a swallow — all of which fail. When the suitors (and the Emperor) are all rebuffed, Kaguya-hime reveals that she is from the Moon — the armies of Heaven descend to return her, and she ascends to the Moon, leaving the grieving Emperor a letter and the elixir of immortality, which he orders burned on the summit of Mount Fuji, the 'mountain nearest Heaven'.

The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter is the founding text of Japanese mono no aware aesthetics — the beauty of transience and loss — and the source of Japan's most enduring cultural image: the Moon as the origin of celestial beings and the destination of the soul.
